title: jnana — Shankara's *Atmabodha*
hook: a short Sanskrit poem says action can't remove ignorance, any more than sweeping can remove the dark

segments.voice: Yesterday: bhakti, and four teachers in the Narada Bhakti Sutras: worship, the stories, delight, and Narada's own, the ache of forgetting. Did you offer one ordinary action? Day six hundred ninety-five.

Walk into a dark room. You could sweep it. You could scrub the floor, rearrange the furniture, work there all night. None of it removes the dark. One thing does, and it takes no effort at all: the light. That picture sits near the beginning of a short Sanskrit poem called the Atmabodha, knowledge of the Self, which tradition gives to Shankara. Today the third strand of this lineage track: after karma, the path of action, and bhakti, the path of love, jnana, the path of knowing.
screen: `A DARK ROOM.` → `SWEEPING WON'T HELP.` → `THE THIRD STRAND: JNANA.`

segments.voice: The Atmabodha is short, under seventy verses, a kind of pocket handbook of Advaita Vedanta, the teaching that the Self and Brahman are not two. Tradition credits it to Shankara; some scholars question whether he wrote it, and it's often studied as a beginner's text. The first verse says who it's for: people whose faults have been worn down by discipline, who are calm, free of craving, and long for freedom. So it starts where the karma days left off: a life of work has prepared the mind. Then the second verse makes its claim. Just as fire is what actually cooks the food, the poem says, knowledge, not any other practice, is what directly brings liberation. Verse three gives the reason. Action isn't opposed to ignorance, so action can't destroy it. Knowledge is opposed to it, the way light is opposed to darkness. And verse four: because of ignorance, the Self seems limited; when ignorance goes, the Self shines on its own, like the sun when the clouds pass. The word jnana means knowing, from the root jna, to know. But it doesn't mean collecting facts. It's closer to the moment you see that the thing you feared was never there. Here the schools of Vedanta take different roads. Shankara's school holds that knowledge alone liberates, and that action and devotion ready the mind for it. Teachers in Ramanuja's tradition hold that devotion to the Lord, supported by knowledge, is the way. Both are living Hindu paths, and many Hindus walk a little of all three.
screen: `FOR THE CALM WHO LONG TO BE FREE.` · `FIRE COOKS; KNOWLEDGE FREES.` · `LIGHT, NOT SWEEPING, ENDS THE DARK.` · `THE SUN BEHIND THE CLOUDS.` · then, large: `JNANA: KNOWING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let the breath be easy. Notice something simple: you're aware. Sounds come and go, and you're aware of them. Thoughts come and go, and you're aware of them. Feelings in the body come and go. Don't chase any of them. Just rest as the one who notices, the way the sky stays while the clouds cross it. If you drift, that's fine; noticing the drift is the practice too. The bell holds the time.
Jnana. Knowing, from the root to know. In the Atmabodha, the light that ends the dark of ignorance.
Your line: jnana — Shankara's Atmabodha. Today, when a worry looms, ask once: is this a snake, or just a shadow I haven't put the light on? Day six hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: In Advaita Vedanta circles, the Atmabodha is often among the first texts a student reads with a teacher, verse by verse, alongside listening, reflection and meditation on the teaching. Many Hindus combine study like this with work done as service and with devotion.

original.note: Sanskrit jñāna, knowing, from the root jñā, to know; the title Ātmabodha (आत्मबोध) means awakening to the Self.

trapdoor: what you thought: jnana means book learning.
what it means: it's knowing the Self directly, the light that ends ignorance.
what a scholar hears: Atmabodha 2–4 argue knowledge, not action, is opposed to avidya; Shankara's authorship is traditional and debated.

sources.ref: Ramanuja's view of bhakti and knowledge (Vishishtadvaita), in general

notes: Verse count: editions give about 67–68 verses; the script says 'under seventy'.
Shankara's authorship of the Atmabodha is traditional; some scholars question it. Confirm wording.
The dark-room/sweeping image elaborates verse 3 (action is not opposed to ignorance; knowledge destroys it as light destroys darkness); the sweeping detail is the script's illustration.
The characterization of Ramanuja's position (devotion supported by knowledge as the means) is brief; a Shri Vaishnava Keeper should check it.
Carry's snake/shadow image echoes the classic Advaita rope-snake example, which is not claimed to be in Atmabodha 1–4.
